content: Inflammation and swelling of the facial nerve are believed to play a role in the development of Bell's palsy. Corticosteroids, due to their strong anti-inflammatory properties, are hypothesized to reduce nerve damage in this condition. This review is an updated analysis of the effectiveness and safety of corticosteroid therapy for Bell's palsy, originally published in 2002 and last updated in 2010. To evaluate the impact of corticosteroids, a systematic search was conducted on March 4, 2016, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS. Additional trials were identified through bibliographic reviews and consultation with experts. Clinical trial registries were also searched for ongoing studies. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials comparing corticosteroid or adrenocorticotrophic hormone therapy to a control group that did not receive effective treatment for Bell's palsy. The primary outcome of interest was incomplete recovery of facial motor function, defined as residual facial weakness. Secondary outcomes included persistent cosmetic sequelae, motor synkinesis (involuntary facial movements), autonomic dysfunction (e.g., hemifacial spasm, crocodile tears), and adverse effects of corticosteroid therapy. Seven trials involving 895 participants were included in the analysis. One of these trials was newly added since the last review. The older, smaller studies had some unclear or high risks of bias, while the larger studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias. Among participants treated with corticosteroids, 79 out of 452 (17%) experienced incomplete recovery of facial motor function six months or more after randomization. This was significantly lower than the 125 out of 447 (28%) in the control group, with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.63 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.50 to 0.80). The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one case of incomplete recovery was 10 (95% CI 6 to 20). The proportion of participants with cosmetically disabling sequelae six months after randomization was similar between the corticosteroid and placebo groups (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.40 to 2.29, based on two trials with 75 participants, low-quality evidence). However, corticosteroid therapy significantly reduced the incidence of motor synkinesis during follow-up (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.91, based on three trials with 485 participants, moderate-quality evidence). Three studies explicitly reported no adverse effects directly attributable to corticosteroids. One trial noted temporary sleep disturbances in three participants receiving prednisolone. Two trials provided detailed accounts of adverse effects in 93 participants, all of which were non-serious. A combined analysis of data from these three trials found no significant difference in the rate of adverse effects between the corticosteroid and placebo groups (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.51, n = 715). In conclusion, moderateto high-quality evidence from randomized controlled trials demonstrates a significant benefit of corticosteroid therapy in the treatment of Bell's palsy.
